## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a19-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Layers</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="raster">raster</span> layer gives every cell of one grid a number or a class: slope, wind, land price, protected or not.</dd>
<dt>Exclusions</dt><dd>An <span class="lx-term" data-term="exclusion-layer">exclusion layer</span> removes land a rule forbids, whatever else it offers.</dd>
<dt>Weights</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="weighted-overlay">weighted overlay</span> adds criterion scores; the weights are value choices, so state them and test others.</dd>
<dt>Sites</dt><dd>Blocks with enough buildable land are ranked by score; a score ranks, a cost model prices.</dd>
<dt>Lines</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="least-cost-path">least-cost path</span> over a <span class="lx-term" data-term="cost-surface">cost surface</span> routes a new line to a substation with room.</dd>
<dt>Limits</dt><dd>Cell size, the date of each layer and whose weights were used can each change the short list.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The arithmetic behind the map</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

| Step | Formula | In this lesson |
|---|---|---|
| A criterion's score | $s = 1 - \min\!\big(1, \max(0, \tfrac{d - d_0}{d_1 - d_0})\big)$ | near a substation: 1 at 0 km, 0 from 15 km (solar) |
| Suitability | $S = \sum_k w_k s_k \,/\, \sum_k w_k$ | default solar weights 20, 35, 15, 20, 10 |
| Room in a block | $B = \sum_c a_c f_c \ge$ the land needed | 150 × 1.29 × 4.2 = 812.7 acres ≈ 3.29 km² of a 4 km² block |
| A line's cost | $\sum_\text{steps} \tfrac{c_u + c_v}{2}\,\ell$ | $c$ ≈ $1,095,979 per km on farmland (2025 dollars), × 1.8 in [flood zones]{.lx-term term="flood-zone"} |

- **Scores.** $d$ is a distance in km and $d_0$, $d_1$ the ramp's ends; $w_k$ is a weight and $s_k$ a score from 0 to 1.
- **Blocks.** $a_c$ is a cell's area in km² and $f_c$ its share outside setbacks, checked at 16 points.
- **Lines.** $c_u$ and $c_v$ are two neighbouring cells' costs per km; the step $\ell$ is 1 km, or $\sqrt{2}$ km on a diagonal.
- **Resources** are rescaled from the region's lowest (0) to its highest (1); land price falls from 1 at $2,500 an acre to 0 at $15,000.
- **The line's cost per km** is NREL's $1,615,100 a mile (2022 dollars) × 128.893 / 118.026 (BEA's GDP deflator, to 2025 dollars) ÷ 1.609344 km a mile.
- **Ties.** Equal scores go to the more northern, then the more western block. Equal-cost paths may differ in their steps but share their length and cost; the page draws the first found.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>From a screen to a supply curve</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **The notebook** (above) rebuilds every layer as a NumPy array from the same seed, then masks, scores, ranks blocks and runs Dijkstra's algorithm for the line.
- **Real layers** come as rasters and vectors in different coordinate systems, with gaps and errors; the notebook cleans and aligns simulated ones onto one grid.
- **Areas and distances.** An equal-area projection keeps areas true, not distances: check its distance error where you measure setbacks and routes, or measure on the curved Earth (geodesic distances).
- **A supply curve** sorts many sites by their cost, as NREL's supply curves do for about 67,000 cells of 11.5 km × 11.5 km, and hands it to a planning model such as [M3](m03-capacity-expansion.html).
- **Out of this course's scope:** remote sensing, geostatistics, cartography and field surveys.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>The data-center card: spare capacity and the cost of waiting</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>A campus near a substation without <span class="lx-term" data-term="spare-capacity">spare capacity</span> waits for an upgrade. In step 7, that wait has no price; one study prices it.</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:code"><p>A late grid connection costs the developer lost <span class="lx-term" data-term="margin">margin</span> and <span class="lx-term" data-term="carrying-cost">carrying costs</span>; ratepayers face utility carrying and <span class="lx-term" data-term="stranded-cost">stranding</span> costs; society bears <span class="lx-term" data-term="external-cost">external costs</span>.</p><p>The study keeps these present-value accounts separate.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2026), accepted paper, 2026 North American Power Symposium (NAPS); DOI pending.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">Holds when: the delay is given and the inputs are illustrative. Leaves out: why service is late.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">The full case: case file <a href="cf7-cost-of-waiting.html">CF7</a>; how a large load asks for service: <a href="a06-interconnection.html">A6</a>.</p>

<li>Rights-of-way of existing roads and lines, airports, radar, wetlands beyond the flood zone, and wildlife surveys.</li>
<li>Two projects on one substation: each site here is screened alone, so they could both claim its spare capacity.</li>
<li>Grid studies: whether the network beyond the substation can take the power or the load.</li>
<li>Lease payments to landowners, taxes, and the plant's own cost, which is the same at every site.</li>
<li>Where the data center's water comes from, and how much its cooling uses.</li>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a19-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cheap" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The site with the highest suitability score is the cheapest to build.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Wind site A costs $16.6 million up front, site E $12.4 million. A score mixes criteria by chosen weights; a cost model prices them.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="weight" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Excluding land and giving it a low weight do the same job.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Priced at about $41,500 a mile (NREL's $38,000 in 2022 dollars), the new line crossed 3.4 km of protected land; only the exclusion kept it out.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="sun" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Sunshine differs by only 4.5% across this region, so it barely moves a solar site's score.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Min–max scaling stretches the 4.5% to a full 0 to 1: at weight 20, sunshine spreads blocks' scores by about 19 points, more than cheap land's 17. Scaling and weights, not physics, set that.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="res" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A map of 1 km cells can check a 220 m setback.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A setback is smaller than a cell: this map checks 16 points in each cell, and NREL's supply curves check setbacks on 90 m cells.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a19">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="rule" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A county forbids turbines within 400 m of any home. In a screening study, that rule is best treated as…</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">an exclusion layer</li><li data-value="b">a low weight on “away from homes”</li><li data-value="c">a cost per km</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>An exclusion: it is a rule, so no other advantage of a site may outvote it.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="date" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Your homes layer is dated 2019 and it is now 2025. What can go wrong?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Newer homes inside setbacks or next to a site are missed</li><li data-value="b">The wind speeds change</li><li data-value="c">Nothing: homes rarely change</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Newer homes are missed. In step 8, 36 homes built since 2019 push solar site A out of the top five.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card a19-practice">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 30 minutes on your own</p>
<ol class="lx-fb-practice">
<li><p><b>A score by hand.</b> One cell's scores and the default weights are below. What is its suitability, out of 100?</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts a19-pr" data-practice="score"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Criterion</th><th scope="col">Score, 0 to 1</th><th scope="col">Weight</th><th scope="col">Neighbours' weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Sunshine</th><td class="n">0.6</td><td class="n">20</td><td class="n">10</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Near a substation</th><td class="n">0.9</td><td class="n">35</td><td class="n">10</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Near a road</th><td class="n">1.0</td><td class="n">15</td><td class="n">5</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Cheap land</th><td class="n">0.4</td><td class="n">20</td><td class="n">5</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Away from homes</th><td class="n">0.5</td><td class="n">10</td><td class="n">70</td></tr></tbody></table></div><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>(0.6 × 20 + 0.9 × 35 + 1.0 × 15 + 0.4 × 20 + 0.5 × 10) ÷ 100 = 0.715, or 71.5 out of 100.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Other weights.</b> Score the same cell with the neighbours' weights, the table's last column.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>(0.6 × 10 + 0.9 × 10 + 1.0 × 5 + 0.4 × 5 + 0.5 × 70) ÷ 100 = 0.57, or 57 out of 100: lower, because this cell is close to homes.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Land for solar.</b> A 200 MW (AC) farm has 1.3 MW of panels per MW of inverters. At LBNL's 4.2 acres per MW of panels, how much land do the arrays need?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>200 × 1.3 × 4.2 = 1,092 acres, about 4.42 km²; the whole site is larger (roads, fences, setbacks).</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Land for wind.</b> A 100 MW wind farm takes NREL's average 34.5 ha per MW. How large is it, and how much do turbines, roads and substations occupy for good, at 0.3 ha per MW?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>3,450 ha (34.5 km²) in all; 30 ha for good, under 1%: farming goes on between the turbines.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Setbacks.</b> 40 farmsteads, none within 800 m of another. How much land does a 400 m setback remove, and how much a 220 m one?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>40 × π × 0.4² ≈ 20.1 km² against 40 × π × 0.22² ≈ 6.1 km²: the area grows with the square of the setback.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A line's cost.</b> A 12 km route crosses 8 km of farmland and 4 km of flood zone (× 1.8). Price it in 2025 dollars: NREL's $1,615,100 a mile (2022), deflator 128.893 ÷ 118.026.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$1,615,100 × 128.893 ÷ 118.026 ÷ 1.609344 ≈ $1,095,979 a km; × (8 + 4 × 1.8) ≈ $16.7 million in 2025 dollars.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A least-cost path by hand.</b> Each step goes to a side-by-side cell and costs the two cells' average (costs per km below). What is the cheapest path from top left to bottom right?</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts a19-pr" data-practice="grid"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Row</th><th scope="col">Left</th><th scope="col">Middle</th><th scope="col">Right</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Top</th><td class="n">1</td><td class="n">1</td><td class="n">4</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Middle</th><td class="n">1</td><td class="n">5</td><td class="n">1</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Bottom</th><td class="n">2</td><td class="n">1</td><td class="n">1</td></tr></tbody></table></div><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Down the left column, then along the bottom row: 1 + 1.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 5. Along the top row and down the right column costs 7.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Read a claim critically.</b> A report says: “Our map shows the best solar site in the county.” What four questions would you ask?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Whose weights, and would other weights pick another site; which land was excluded, by what rule; how fine and how recent the layers are; who was asked, and what a visit found.</p></details></li>
</ol>
</div>
```
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>NREL's 2024 supply curves screen the contiguous U.S. the same way: exclusions and local setbacks on 90 m cells, about 67,000 candidate sites of 11.5 km × 11.5 km, and least-cost paths to the grid.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Where its median setbacks become the 90th percentile of local rules, much less land is left: the rules are local choices.</p>
</div>
```
